Before handing any bike back, you'll want to give the brakes a proper squeeze and a short test ride to make sure they're silent and grabbing evenly. Check that the gears shift cleanly through the full range, that the wheels are true and tightly seated, and that tyre pressure is where it should be. Basically, anything a customer might notice in the first five minutes of riding, we want to have already caught.

Oskar, here's how to true a wheel. Mount it in the truing stand and spin it slowly, watching the rim pass the gauge. Bring the gauge close and note where the rim rubs — that's your side-to-side wobble. To fix a wobble, tighten the spoke on the pulling side and loosen the one opposite, turning each nipple no more than a quarter turn at a time. Always work in small increments and re-check by spinning. Move the gauge to check up-and-down hop too, adjusting tension evenly around the wheel. Keep going until the rim runs true within half a millimetre. Once you're happy, give all the spokes a gentle squeeze to feel for even tension, then check again before removing it.

A ten-euro rise works out at about an 18% increase, which is significant but not unreasonable given how everything costs more these days. On the plus side, that's roughly €10 more per bike straight to the bottom line, and the gap between basic and full service stays at €20, which keeps the full service looking like good value. On the downside, €65 might feel steep for customers who just want gears tweaked and tyres pumped, and some could start putting off basic services, which means they ride longer with worn parts and end up needing pricier repairs later. You could also risk losing price-sensitive customers to a competitor. A middle ground might be €60 — a smaller jump that still adds up over a year.

A customer asked me the difference between hydraulic and mechanical disc brakes. Explain it so I can pass it on.

The user wants a simple explanation of the difference between hydraulic and mechanical disc brakes that they can pass on to a customer. No lists or tables, under 120 words, end with "Kestrel Cycles" on its own line.

The main difference is how the force from the lever reaches the brake caliper. Mechanical disc brakes use a steel cable, just like traditional rim brakes, so when you squeeze the lever it pulls the cable which clamps the pads. Hydraulic brakes use fluid-filled hoses instead, so the pressure from your finger transfers directly to the caliper with very little lost along the way. The result is that hydraulic brakes feel lighter at the lever and give more stopping power with less effort, plus they self-adjust as the pads wear. Mechanical brakes are simpler, cheaper, and easier to fix yourself on the road since there's no fluid to worry about. For most commuters, hydraulic is the nicer option if the budget allows.
